title: Starting from nothing
hook: refugee Sikhs rebuilt lives in Delhi and East Punjab

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nankana Sahib, and your line was left behind. Did you say the name of a place you can't go back to? Today, the people who arrived with nothing. Day one thousand four.

What do you sell when everything you owned is on the other side of a border? A few combs, some bars of soap, a row of pencils, laid out on a wooden crate turned upside down on a Delhi pavement. Behind the crate, a man in a turban who, a few months earlier, owned land or a shop in a town that is now in Pakistan. Stories like this are told in Punjabi families: a grandfather who sold things off a crate, a grandmother who sewed through the night, a camp of tents, a first rented room. The refugees came into Delhi and East Punjab carrying what they could hold. Then they started again.
screen: `A CRATE ON A DELHI PAVEMENT.` → `COMBS, SOAP, PENCILS.` → `THEN THEY STARTED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the arrival. Families who had crossed the border lived in camps, in shelters, in the homes of relatives already crowded. Land, shops and houses were gone. Some had lost people too, and carried that along with the bundles. Second, the work. Sikh teaching sums up a life in three short instructions often traced to Guru Nanak: remember the Name, earn by honest work, and share what you have. Naam japo, kirat karo, vand chhako. The middle one is kirat, honest labor. In the stories families tell of those years, it was the thing they could still hold on to when nothing else was left. A crate became a stall, a stall a shop, a shop a living. Third, the Guru's measure. Early on this path you met Bhai Lalo, the carpenter of Saidpur. Tradition says Guru Nanak ate Lalo's coarse bread, earned by his own hands, and turned down a rich man's feast. Not the one who had the most. The one who worked honestly and shared. Fourth, the sharing. In the stories of those years, langar was cooked even in the camps: the free kitchen, now feeding people who had nothing, sometimes cooked by people who had very little more. Starting over and giving away turned out not to be opposites. That's today's line: from nothing. Not nothing at all. From nothing but hands, honest work, and a shared pot.
screen: `CAMPS, SHELTERS, CROWDED ROOMS.` · `KIRAT KARO: EARN BY HONEST WORK.` · `LALO'S BREAD: EARNED, AND SHARED.` · `LANGAR IN THE CAMPS.` · then, large: `FROM NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a beginning. Sit, and let your hands rest open. Think of one thing you've wanted to start and haven't, because you didn't feel ready: a skill, a garden, a savings jar, a letter, an apology. Don't plan the whole of it. Find only the very first step, small enough to do today with what you already have. Breathe in, and see your hands doing it. Breathe out, and let go of waiting for the perfect start. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Kirat, honest work: kirat karo, earn by honest labor. The refugees of Partition rebuilding their lives in Delhi and East Punjab, with honest work and shared bread. Today's word.
Your line: from nothing. Today, take the first small step of that one thing, with what you already have. Day one thousand four.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karo, earning by honest work, alongside naam japo and vand chhako, and Punjabi families descended from Partition refugees retell how their elders rebuilt their lives.
